title: COZAAR (losartan potassium) tablets, for oral use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 9, effective 20 January 2026, label text revised 6/2021
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Organon LLC.
result: Initial US approval 1995. Indications: hypertension in adults and children older than 6 years; reduction of the risk of stroke in patients with hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy, with the statement that there is evidence that this benefit does not apply to Black patients; and treatment of diabetic nephropathy with raised serum creatinine and proteinuria (urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 300 mg/g or more) in patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of hypertension. Boxed warning, fetal toxicity: when pregnancy is detected, discontinue as soon as possible; drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus; second- and third-trimester use reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death, with oligohydramnios, fetal lung hypoplasia, skeletal deformations including skull hypoplasia, hypotension, anuria, renal failure and death. Mechanism: losartan and its principal active metabolite block the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II by selectively blocking its binding to the AT1 receptor found in many tissues, for example vascular smooth muscle and adrenal gland; neither shows partial agonist activity at AT1, and both have about 1000-fold greater affinity for AT1 than for AT2; losartan is a reversible competitive inhibitor of AT1 in vitro and the active metabolite, 10 to 40 times more potent by weight, appears to be a reversible non-competitive inhibitor; neither inhibits ACE (kininase II, the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin), nor binds or blocks other hormone receptors or ion channels important in cardiovascular regulation. Pharmacodynamics: a 100 mg dose inhibits the pressor effect of angiotensin II by about 85% at peak, with 25% to 40% inhibition persisting for 24 hours; removal of angiotensin II negative feedback causes a doubling to tripling of plasma renin activity; losartan does not affect the response to bradykinin, whereas ACE inhibitors increase the response to bradykinin; aldosterone plasma concentrations fall, yet very little effect on serum potassium was observed; no apparent rebound effect follows abrupt withdrawal. Pharmacokinetics: systemic bioavailability about 33%; peak concentrations of losartan at 1 hour and of the active metabolite at 3 to 4 hours, with the metabolite AUC about 4 times that of losartan; terminal half-life about 2 hours for losartan and 6 to 9 hours for the metabolite; about 14% of an oral dose is converted to the active metabolite; in vitro studies indicate that cytochrome P450 2C9 and 3A4 are involved in the biotransformation of losartan, and the data suggest that conversion to the active metabolite is mediated primarily by P450 2C9 and not P450 3A4; subjects who do not metabolise losartan to the active metabolite have been shown to have a specific, rare defect in cytochrome P450 2C9; fluconazole, an inhibitor of P450 2C9, decreased the AUC of the active metabolite by approximately 40% and increased the AUC of losartan by approximately 70% after multiple doses, rifampicin decreased the AUC of losartan and of the active metabolite by 30% and 40%, and conversion after intravenous administration was not affected by the P450 3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole; the pharmacodynamic consequences of concomitant use of losartan and inhibitors of P450 2C9 have not been examined; plasma concentrations and AUCs of losartan and the metabolite are 50% to 90% higher in mild or moderate renal insufficiency and neither is removed by haemodialysis; in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment concentrations of losartan and of the metabolite were about 5 times and 1.7 times those in healthy volunteers, so the recommended starting dose is 25 mg. Hyperkalaemia: monitor serum potassium periodically and treat appropriately; dosage reduction or discontinuation may be required; concomitant drugs that raise serum potassium may lead to hyperkalaemia. Cough: in two prospective, parallel-group, double-blind randomised trials in hypertensive patients who had had typical ACE-inhibitor cough on challenge with lisinopril and whose cough disappeared on placebo, the incidence of cough during up to 8 weeks of double-blind treatment was, in study 1 (n=135; 89% Caucasian, 64% female), 25% with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, 17% with losartan 50 mg and 69% with lisinopril 20 mg, and in study 2 (n=97; 90% Caucasian, 51% female), 35% with placebo, 29% with losartan and 62% with lisinopril; cases of cough, including positive re-challenges, have been reported with losartan after marketing. Angio-oedema, including swelling of the larynx and glottis causing airway obstruction, swelling of the face, lips, pharynx or tongue and swelling of the intestine, has been reported after marketing; some of these patients had previously experienced angio-oedema with other drugs, including ACE inhibitors. LIFE study: 9193 hypertensive patients with electrocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy randomised to losartan 50 mg or atenolol 50 mg once daily, with hydrochlorothiazide added and the dose doubled as needed; mean age 67 years, 54% female, 533 (6%) Black, baseline blood pressure 174/98 mmHg in both groups, mean follow-up 4.8 years; the primary composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal stroke or non-fatal myocardial infarction occurred in 508 (11%; 23.8 per 1000 patient-years) on losartan against 588 (13%; 27.9 per 1000 patient-years) on atenolol, a 13% risk reduction (95% CI 2% to 23%, p=0.021) adjusted for baseline Framingham risk score and degree of left ventricular hypertrophy; fatal or non-fatal stroke 232 (5%; 10.8 per 1000 patient-years) against 309 (7%; 14.5), a 25% reduction (11% to 37%, p=0.001); fatal or non-fatal myocardial infarction 198 (4%) against 188 (4%), risk reduction -7% (p=0.491); end-of-study mean blood pressure 144.1/81.3 against 145.4/80.9 mmHg. In the subgroup of 533 Black patients there were 46 primary endpoints among 270 patients (17%; 42 per 1000 patient-years) on losartan and 29 among 263 (11%; 26 per 1000 patient-years) on atenolol; the label states that this finding could not be explained by differences other than race or by imbalance between treatment groups, that blood-pressure reductions were consistent between Black and non-Black patients, that it cannot be known whether the observed difference is the result of chance, and that the LIFE study provides no evidence that the benefit applies to Black patients. RENAAL study: 1513 patients with type 2 diabetes and nephropathy randomised to losartan 50 mg once daily, titrated to 100 mg, or placebo on a background of conventional antihypertensive therapy excluding ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II antagonists; mean follow-up 3.4 years; the primary composite of doubling of serum creatinine, end-stage renal disease or death occurred in 43.5% against 47.1%, a 16.1% risk reduction (95% CI 2.3% to 27.9%, p=0.022); overall incidence of doubling of serum creatinine 21.6% against 26.0% (25.3% reduction, 7.8% to 39.4%, p=0.006), end-stage renal disease 19.6% against 25.5% (28.6% reduction, 11.5% to 42.4%, p=0.002) and death 21.0% against 20.3% (p=0.884); end-of-study mean blood pressure 143/76 against 146/77 mmHg; adverse events reported in 4% or more of treated patients and with a 2% or greater difference against placebo included asthenia or fatigue, chest pain, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea, anaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, back pain, muscular weakness and urinary tract infection. Dual blockade: in VA NEPHRON-D, 1448 patients with type 2 diabetes, raised urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30 to 89.9 ml/min were randomised to lisinopril or placebo on a background of losartan and followed for a median 2.2 years; the combination gave no additional benefit for the composite of decline in GFR, end-stage renal disease or death and increased hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. In four placebo-controlled monotherapy trials of 10 to 150 mg per day, doses of 50, 100 and 150 mg once daily lowered blood pressure by 5.5 to 10.5 mmHg systolic and 3.5 to 7.5 mmHg diastolic more than placebo, with no greater effect at 150 mg; the effect was somewhat less in Black patients, usually a low-renin population.
